excluded.title: TranSPArent: Taint-style Vulnerability Detection in Generic Single Page Applications through Automated Framework Abstraction
excluded.title_norm: transparent taint-style vulnerability detection in generic single page applications through automated framework abstraction
excluded.reason: Surfaced from Yinzhi Cao's own 2026 publication list (JHU) while checking the Buzz to Boom promotion trigger, then confirmed on the NDSS '26 accepted list. Diwangkara & Cao. Automatically abstracts SPA frameworks (Vue, React, Angular) via static+dynamic analysis to recover framework-specific taint sinks, then runs end-to-end static dataflow detection: 19 intermediate SPA sinks recovered (14 absent from the CodeQL standard library), 11 zero-days in GitHub repos (one with 24k+ stars / 30M requests/month), 4 fixed or acknowledged. Matched the config keywords 'dom-based' / 'taint' but the target is BROWSER-RENDERED web SPAs; sinks are insecure DOM APIs inside the browser sandbox, worst case is web XSS. No Electron / Node.js-runtime / renderer-main IPC / preload / desktop-privilege angle -> EXCLUDE 'pure web-app XSS with no desktop/Electron angle'. Notable as lineage only: same senior author as the (context-only) Buzz to Boom Electron fuzzing preprint, and its framework-abstraction idea is a plausible methodological analogue for abstracting Electron's IPC/contextBridge surface.

excluded.title: DOM-XSS Detection via Webpage Interaction Fuzzing and URL Component Synthesis
excluded.title_norm: dom-xss detection via webpage interaction fuzzing and url component synthesis
excluded.reason: Surfaced on the NDSS '26 accepted list during a re-sweep (missed by earlier NDSS '26 passes). Sabino, Cassel, Abreu, Adao, Bauer, Jia (CMU / IST Lisboa) - i.e. the SAME TEAM as the in-scope NodeMedic-FINE (NDSS '25). Presents SWIPE: fuzzes user interactions to trigger event handlers plus dynamic symbolic execution to synthesize URL GET parameters/fragments; run over 44,480 URLs from Tranco top-30,000 domains, finds 15% more vulnerabilities than prior work and 20 new vulnerabilities from synthesized URL components. Matched the config keywords 'dom-based' / 'xss' but is pure in-browser DOM-XSS on ordinary web pages - no desktop app, no Node.js privilege surface, no escalation past the browser sandbox -> EXCLUDE 'pure web-app XSS with no desktop/Electron angle'. Recorded permanently because 'DOM-XSS' is a standing query term that will keep re-surfacing it. Still citable as a methodological reference for interaction-driven fuzzing of DOM sinks, which is the browser-side analogue of driving an Electron renderer.

excluded.title: The First Large-Scale Systematic Study of Python Class Pollution Vulnerability
excluded.title_norm: the first large-scale systematic study of python class pollution vulnerability
excluded.reason: Confirmed on the IEEE S&P '26 accepted-papers page. Liu, Zhong, Yu, Lyu, Kang, Cao (JHU) - note Jianjia Yu and Zhengyu Liu are also Buzz to Boom / UoP authors. Presents Pyrl, a static operational taint analysis over 'get'/'set' primitives yielding a 6-type taxonomy of Python class pollution; applied to >500,000 Python programs from GitHub and PyPI, finds 47 zero-day exploitable class pollutions (incl. Microsoft Azure CLI and Google Mesop, both patched), 5 developer fixes, 7 CVEs assigned. Matched the config keyword 'prototype pollution' as its direct PYTHON analogue, but the language, runtime and ecosystem are Python/PyPI throughout - no JavaScript prototype chain, no Node.js runtime, no Electron/desktop angle -> outside the INCLUDE scope (npm/supply-chain *as it affects Electron or the Node.js runtime*). Same rationale as the excluded PyPI items (ACSAC'23 npm/PyPI malicious packages, USENIX Sec'26 PyGuard, ESORICS'26 'Short Paths, Real Risks'). Useful to the thesis only as a cross-language framing citation: pollution-class bugs generalize beyond JS prototypes.

excluded.title: Kintsugi: Empowering LLMs to Mitigate Web Vulnerabilities via Runtime Policy Injection
excluded.title_norm: kintsugi empowering llms to mitigate web vulnerabilities via runtime policy injection
excluded.reason: Reviewed and deliberately not ledgered on 08-04 and 08-06 because no abstract had been released; the USENIX Sec '26 Technical Sessions page now publishes abstracts ahead of PDFs, so this is finally decidable and is being recorded permanently to stop it re-surfacing. Peng Yihao et al. (Tsinghua). Automated runtime containment for the 'response gap' between vulnerability detection and patching: differential syscall analysis on normal vs. malicious requests to localize vulnerability-related functions, an LLM to delineate the offending code snippet and set policy trigger points, then a least-privilege syscall whitelist enforced via eBPF and cgroups, activated only when execution enters the protected snippet. Evaluated on 27 real-world CVEs across PHP, Python and Java; 7.6 min average response time, 9.2% latency overhead on targeted APIs, 2.21% throughput drop on concurrent traffic. Matched only the generic escalation keyword 'remote code execution'; it is server-side WEB-application defense on PHP/Python/Java stacks -> EXCLUDE 'pure web-app XSS with no desktop/Electron angle'. No Electron / Node.js / renderer-main IPC / preload / desktop angle anywhere in the abstract.

excluded.title: From Obfuscated to Obvious: A Comprehensive JavaScript Deobfuscation Tool for Security Analysis
excluded.title_norm: from obfuscated to obvious a comprehensive javascript deobfuscation tool for security analysis
excluded.reason: Surfaced on the NDSS '26 accepted list (A-P range) during this run's re-sweep; never previously ledgered. Zhou, Ying, Chai, Wang (Beijing Univ. of Posts and Telecommunications + QI-ANXIN Technology Research Institute). Presents JSIMPLIFIER, a multi-stage JavaScript deobfuscation pipeline (preprocessing -> AST-based static analysis -> dynamic execution tracing -> LLM-enhanced identifier renaming) plus multi-dimensional evaluation metrics (control/data-flow, code simplification, entropy, LLM-based readability). Releases the largest real-world obfuscated-JS dataset to date: 44,421 samples (23,212 wild malicious + 21,209 benign); reports 100% processing capability across 20 obfuscation techniques, 100% correctness on evaluation subsets, 88.2% code-complexity reduction, and >4x readability improvement. Matched only the generic 'javascript' vocabulary: the target is obfuscated JS delivered on the WEB / in malware samples, analyzed for readability, with no Electron / Node.js-runtime / renderer-main IPC / preload / desktop-privilege angle -> outside the INCLUDE scope. Recorded permanently because JS-analysis queries will keep re-surfacing it. Retains genuine METHODOLOGICAL value to the thesis, however: packaged Electron apps ship bundled/minified (and sometimes obfuscated) JS inside app.asar, so any static or taint analysis of a shipped Electron app faces exactly this preprocessing problem - JSIMPLIFIER is a citable off-the-shelf front-end for that step, and its 44,421-sample dataset is a ready benchmark. Same handling as the excluded CCS'23 'Jack-in-the-box' JS-bundling study.

context_non_venue.title: Buzz to Boom: Detecting Message Progression Vulnerabilities in Electron Applications via Segmented Directed Fuzzing
context_non_venue.title_norm: buzz to boom detecting message progression vulnerabilities in electron applications via segmented directed fuzzing
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron vulnerability discovery — most thesis-central out-of-venue item to date)
context_non_venue.why: Strongest out-of-venue candidate this watch has surfaced: a segmented directed fuzzing framework (Proton) that DISCOVERS zero-day vulnerabilities in real Electron apps — the exact thesis topic, not merely Node.js-runtime-adjacent. Defines a new bug class, Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs): attacker-controlled inputs that chain across processes via message passing to reach privileged/terminal sinks (OS command execution). Explicitly positions past prior Electron work (unsafe-config + malicious-DOM studies, i.e. DOM-tree type/Inspectron/COINDEF) as unable to detect these cross-process, multi-step exploits. Evaluated on 589 real Electron apps → 23 zero-day MPVs, 22 to full RCE (projects >50k GitHub stars), 13 acks / 11 fixes / 11 CVEs, Vercel bug bounty on Hyper; 17 more zero-days than end-to-end fuzzing.
context_non_venue.venue_status: arXiv-only v1 (22 Jul 2026), cs.CR. context_non_venue.title: Differential Security Analysis of Cross-Platform Electron Applications
context_non_venue.title_norm: differential security analysis of cross-platform electron applications
context_non_venue.venue: MS thesis, University of Illinois Chicago (advisor Jason Polakis)
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron framework security analysis) — but NOT a peer-reviewed venue
context_non_venue.why: Same-lab successor to Inspectron (USENIX Sec '24): advisor Jason Polakis, committee Chris Kanich (both Inspectron co-authors) + Stefano Zanero. Takes a *differential* angle this watch has not seen at a watched venue — it compares Electron's implementation of web security mechanisms against Google Chrome's, using manual testing plus the Web Platform Tests (WPT) cross-browser suite, and reports significant divergences in CORS, permissions, cookie handling, and especially the notion of an *origin* for local (file://) HTML content and webviews. Reported consequence: third-party web resources can navigate the file system and reach sensitive information; concludes by advocating stricter Electron security defaults. Two reasons it matters to this thesis: (1) it is the clearest example of a *differential-testing* methodology for Electron vulnerability discovery — complementary to Inspectron (black-box config auditing), Proton (directed fuzzing), and COINDEF (defense); (2) it is a master's thesis at the same scope level as the user's, useful as a structural/scoping reference.

No peer-reviewed venue publication found; not at any of the 9 watched venues → context only, NOT added to in_scope[]/excluded[]. context_non_venue.title: Electron upstream security advisories, 2026 (two coordinated batches: CVE-2026-34764..34781 and CVE-2026-70597..70612)
context_non_venue.venue: Electron project / GitHub Security Advisories (GHSA), mirrored in the GitLab Advisory Database and NVD
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron framework vulnerabilities) — but upstream CVEs, not peer-reviewed academic work
context_non_venue.why: Best-grounded real-world motivation material the watch has produced, and the first item that lets the thesis quantify the Electron framework's own vulnerability trend from an authoritative source. GLAD's npm/electron index lists 35 advisories dated 2026 versus 1 in 2025, 2 in 2024 and 5 in 2023 — a step change driven by two coordinated batch disclosures. Most thesis-relevant, all landing squarely on the boundaries this thesis targets: (a) CONTEXT-ISOLATION BYPASSES — CVE-2026-70601 (7.5 HIGH, CWE-693): apps exposing Promise-returning functions via contextBridge (the standard wrapper for ipcRenderer.invoke) let untrusted web content hijack Function.prototype.bind and reach the isolated preload world and every capability it holds, escalating to Node.js access where the renderer is unsandboxed or nodeIntegration is on; CVE-2026-70610 (5.4 MEDIUM, CWE-1321): the contextBridge object-copy path used v8::Object::Set ([[Set]] semantics) in CreateProxyForAPI (shell/renderer/api/electron_api_context_bridge.cc), so a crafted __proto__ property fired the inherited Object.prototype setter and polluted the prototype of objects landing in the privileged preload context — fixed by switching to CreateDataProperty ([[DefineOwnProperty]]), PR #51083, fix commits 2026-04-16, GHSA-ff2p-hmqr-hxm4; CVE-2026-34780 (8.3 HIGH): context-isolation bypass via bridged WebCodecs VideoFrame objects. (b) PROCESS/PRIVILEGE CONFIGURATION — CVE-2026-34769 (7.7 HIGH): an undocumented commandLineSwitches webPreference lets switches be appended to the renderer command line, potentially disabling renderer sandboxing, when webPreferences is built by spreading untrusted config; CVE-2026-34775 (6.8): nodeIntegrationInWorker not correctly scoped in shared renderer processes, so workers in frames set to false could still receive Node.js integration. (c) IPC INTEGRITY — CVE-2026-34778 (5.9): a service worker can spoof reply messages on the internal IPC channel used by webContents.executeJavaScript(), resolving the main-process promise with attacker-controlled data. Why this matters to the argument: CVE-2026-70610 is prototype pollution crossing the context-isolation boundary, which is the missing link between the ledger's Node.js prototype-pollution line (Silent Spring, GHunter, Bullseye, UoP) and Electron proper — the pollution primitive those papers study, landing in Electron's own C++ bridge. And CVE-2026-70601 is a near-repeat of CVE-2023-29198 (contextBridge context-isolation bypass), supporting a recurrence/regression framing. Also closes the 08-07 open item: that run recorded an unverified search-summary claim about CVE-2026-70601; it is now confirmed against GLAD + the Electron GHSA references.
